members.statement_original: Let $\theta_* \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be an unknown signal of interest. Let $\mathsf{G}\subseteq \mathsf{O}(d)$ be a known compact subgroup of the orthogonal group of dimension $d$. We denote by $\Lambda$ the unique Haar probability measure on $\mathsf{G}$, satisfying $$\Lambda(\mathsf{G})=1, \qquad \Lambda(g \cdot S)=\Lambda(S \cdot g)=\Lambda(S),$$ for any $g \in \mathsf{G}$ and Borel measurable subset $S \subseteq \mathsf{G}$.

Let $\mathcal{R}^\mathsf{G}$ be the (real) algebra of all $\mathsf{G}$-invariant polynomial functions $p:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$. These are the polynomials $p$ that satisfy $$p(\theta)=p(g \cdot \theta) \text{ for all }
\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d \text{ and } g \in \mathsf{G}.$$ For each integer $k \geq 0$, let $\mathcal{R}_{\leq k}^\mathsf{G}$ be the subalgebra generated by the $\mathsf{G}$-invariant polynomials having total degree at most $k$. This subalgebra consists of the polynomials $p \in \mathcal{R}^\mathsf{G}$ that may be expressed as $p(\theta)=q(p_1(\theta),\ldots,p_j(\theta))$ for some polynomial $q$ and some $p_1,\ldots,p_j \in \mathcal{R}^\mathsf{G}$ each having degree $\leq k$ (where $p$ itself may have degree larger than $k$).

members.statement_original:
Polynomials $p_1,\ldots,p_k:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ are *algebraically independent* (over $\mathbb{R}$) if there is no nonzero polynomial $q:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $q(p_1(\theta),\ldots,p_k(\theta))$ is identically $0$ for all $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d$.

For any $\mathcal{A}\subseteq \mathcal{R}^\mathsf{G}$, its *transcendence degree* $\mathop{\mathrm{trdeg}}(\mathcal{A})$ is the maximum cardinality of any algebraically independent subset $A \subseteq \mathcal{A}$. Any maximal such subset $A \subseteq \mathcal{A}$ is a *transcendence basis* for $\mathcal{A}$.

In the *unprojected orbit recovery model*, we observe $n$ noisy and rotated samples of $\theta_*$, given by $$Y_i=g_i \cdot \theta_*+\sigma \varepsilon_i \in \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\tag{2.1}$$ where $g_1,\ldots,g_n \overset{iid}{\sim} \Lambda$ are Haar-uniform random elements of $\mathsf{G}$, and $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}_{d
\times d})$ are Gaussian noise vectors independent of $g_1,\ldots,g_n$.

members.statement_original: A subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is *generic* if $\mathbb{R}^d \setminus S$ is contained in the zero set of some nonzero analytic function $\psi:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^k$, for some $k \geq 1$.
The signal $\theta_*$ is identifiable only up to an arbitrary rotation in $\mathsf{G}$, that is, it is identifiable up to its orbit $$\mathcal{O}_{\theta_*}=\{g \cdot \theta_*:\,g \in \mathsf{G}\}.$$

To describe the model, let $f:\mathcal{S}^1 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a periodic function on the unit circle $\mathcal{S}^1 \cong [0,1)$. We identify the rotational group $\mathsf{SO}(2)$ also with $[0,1)$, and represent the rotation of $f$ by an element $\mathfrak{g}\in \mathsf{SO}(2) \cong [0,1)$ as $f_\mathfrak{g}(t)=f(t+\mathfrak{g}\bmod 1)$. Each sample is an observation of the rotated function $f_\mathfrak{g}$ with additive white noise, $$f_\mathfrak{g}(t)+\sigma\,\mathrm{d}W(t),$$ where $\mathfrak{g}\sim \mathop{\mathrm{Unif}}([0,1))$ and $\mathrm{d}W(t)$ denotes a standard Gaussian white noise process on $\mathcal{S}^1$. This may be understood as observing a realization of the Gaussian process $\{F(h)\}_{h \in L_2(\mathcal{S}^1)}=\{\int h(t)[f_\mathfrak{g}(t)\mathrm{d}t+
\sigma \mathrm{d}W(t)]\}_{h \in L_2(\mathcal{S}^1)}$ with mean and covariance functions $$\mathbb{E}[F(h)]=\int_0^1 h(t)f_\mathfrak{g}(t)\mathrm{d}t,
\qquad \mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}[F(h_1),F(h_2)]=\sigma^2 \int_0^1 h_1(t)h_2(t)\,\mathrm{d}t,\tag{3.1}$$ or equivalently as observing all coefficients of $f_\mathfrak{g}$ in a complete orthonormal basis $\{h_j(t)\}_{j=1}^\infty$ of $L_2(\mathcal{S}^1)$ with independent $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ noise for each basis coefficient.

We consider the real Fourier basis on $\mathcal{S}^1$, given by $$h_0(t)=1, \quad h_{l1}(t)=\sqrt{2} \cos 2\pi lt, \quad
h_{l2}(t)=\sqrt{2} \sin 2\pi lt \quad \text{for } l=1,2,3,\ldots.\tag{3.2}$$ We then restrict our model to the finite-dimensional space of functions $f:\mathcal{S}^1 \to \mathbb{R}$ that have finite bandlimit $L \geq 1$ in this basis, that is, $f$ admits a representation $$f(t)=\theta^{(0)}h_0(t)+\sum_{l=1}^L \theta_1^{(l)}h_{l1}(t)+
\sum_{l=1}^L\theta_2^{(l)}h_{l2}(t).\tag{3.3}$$ Importantly, the space of such bandlimited functions is closed under rotations of $\mathcal{S}^1$. Writing $$\theta=(\theta^{(0)},\theta_1^{(1)},\theta_2^{(1)},\ldots,
\theta_1^{(L)},\theta_2^{(L)}) \in \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad d=2L+1$$ for the vector of Fourier coefficients, the rotation $f \mapsto f_\mathfrak{g}$ corresponds to $\theta \mapsto g \cdot \theta$, where $g$ belongs to the block-diagonal representation $$\mathsf{G}=\left\{\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}\left(1,\begin{pmatrix} \cos 2\pi \mathfrak{g}& \sin 2\pi \mathfrak{g}\\
-\sin 2\pi \mathfrak{g}& \cos 2\pi \mathfrak{g}\end{pmatrix},
\ldots,\begin{pmatrix} \cos 2\pi L\mathfrak{g}& \sin 2\pi L\mathfrak{g}\\
-\sin 2\pi L\mathfrak{g}& \cos 2\pi L\mathfrak{g}\end{pmatrix}\right):
\;\mathfrak{g}\in [0,1)\right\}\tag{3.4}$$ of $\mathsf{SO}(2)$. The observation model for the Fourier coefficients of $f$ then takes the form of (2.1), where we observe coordinates of $g \cdot \theta$ with entrywise i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ noise.

members.statement_original: The problem of minimizing a twice-continuously differentiable function $f:\mathcal{V}\to \mathbb{R}$ over a smooth manifold $\mathcal{V}$ is *globally benign* if each point $x \in \mathcal{V}$ where $\nabla f(x)|_{\mathcal{V}}=0$ is either a global minimizer of $f$ over $\mathcal{V}$, or has a direction of strictly negative curvature, $\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x)|_{\mathcal{V}})<0$.

Consider now a function $f:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$, and the action of $\mathsf{SO}(3)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ given by rotation about the origin. Write $f_\mathfrak{g}(x)=f(\mathfrak{g}^{-1} \cdot x)$ for the rotated function. We consider the observation model with samples $$f_\mathfrak{g}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x+\sigma\,\mathrm{d}W(x),$$ where $\mathfrak{g}\in \mathsf{SO}(3)$ is uniformly random for each sample, and $\mathrm{d}W(x)$ is a standard Gaussian white noise process on $\mathbb{R}^3$.

We parametrize the Fourier domain $\mathbb{R}^3$ by spherical coordinates $(\rho,\phi_1,\phi_2)$ with radius $\rho\geq 0$, latitude $\phi_1\in[0,\pi]$ and longitude $\phi_2\in[0,2\pi)$, and decompose $\hat{f}(\rho,\phi_1,\phi_2)$ in a complex basis $\{\hat{j}_{lsm}\}$ given by the product of the complex spherical harmonics $y_{lm}(\phi_1,\phi_2)$ (reviewed in Appendix D.1) with radial functions $z_s(\rho)$: $$\hat{j}_{lsm}(\rho,\phi_1,\phi_2)=z_s(\rho)y_{lm}(\phi_1,\phi_2)
\quad \text{ for } s \geq 1, \quad l \geq 0, \quad m \in \{-l,\ldots,l\}.\tag{4.3}$$ Here $\{z_s:s \geq 1\}$ may be any system of radial basis functions $z_s:[0,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the orthogonality relation $$\int_0^\infty \rho^2 z_s(\rho) z_{s'}(\rho)d\rho=\mathbf{1}\{s=s'\},\tag{4.4}$$ so that $\{\hat{j}_{lsm}\}$ are orthonormal over $L_2(\mathbb{R}^3,\mathbb{C})$. The inverse Fourier transforms $\{j_{lsm}\}$ of $\{\hat{j}_{lsm}\}$ then provide a complex orthonormal basis in the original signal domain of $f$.

Fixing integer bandlimits $L \geq 1$ and $S_0,\ldots,S_L \geq 1$, we define the index set $$\mathcal{I}=\Big\{(l,s,m):0 \leq l \leq L,\; 1 \leq s \leq S_l,\;-l \leq m \leq l
\Big\}, \qquad d=|\mathcal{I}|=\sum_{l=0}^L (2l+1)S_l\tag{4.5}$$ and assume that $f$ is *$(L, S_0, \ldots, S_L)$-bandlimited* in the sense of admitting the finite basis representation $$f=\sum_{(l,s,m) \in \mathcal{I}} u_m^{(ls)} \cdot j_{lsm}, \qquad
u=\big(u_m^{(ls)}:(l,s,m) \in \mathcal{I}\big) \in \mathbb{C}^d.\tag{4.6}$$ This corresponds to modeling the Fourier transform $\hat{f}$ up to the spherical frequency $L$, and up to the radial frequency $S_l$ for each spherical component $l=0,1,\ldots,L$. For real-valued functions $f$, writing $u=\hat{V}^*\theta$ for a unitary transform $\hat{V} \in \mathbb{C}^{d \times d}$ defined explicitly in (D.S31), we then obtain a real sequence representation $$f=\sum_{(l,s,m) \in \mathcal{I}} \theta_m^{(ls)} \cdot h_{lsm}, \qquad
\theta=\big(\theta_m^{(ls)}:(l,s,m) \in \mathcal{I}\big) \in \mathbb{R}^d\tag{4.7}$$ for a real-valued orthonormal basis $\{h_{lsm}\}$. We describe the forms of $h_{lsm}$ and the rotational action on the basis coefficients $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ in Appendix D.3.

members.statement_original:
Let $\mathcal{S}^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be the unit sphere, and let $f:\mathcal{S}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function on this sphere. We parametrize $\mathcal{S}^2$ by the latitude $\phi_1 \in
[0,\pi]$ and longitude $\phi_2 \in [0,2\pi)$. Writing $f_\mathfrak{g}(\phi_1,\phi_2)=f(\mathfrak{g}^{-1} \cdot
(\phi_1,\phi_2))$ for the rotation of the function $f$, we consider the observation model with samples $$f_\mathfrak{g}(\phi_1,\phi_2)\,\mathrm{d}(\phi_1,\phi_2)+\sigma\,\mathrm{d}W(\phi_1,\phi_2),$$ where $\mathfrak{g}\in \mathsf{SO}(3)$ is a uniform random rotation for each sample, $\mathrm{d}(\phi_1,\phi_2)=\sin\phi_1\,\mathrm{d}\phi_1\,\mathrm{d}\phi_2$ denotes the surface area measure on $\mathcal{S}^2$, and $\mathrm{d}W(\phi_1,\phi_2)$ is a standard Gaussian white noise process on $\mathcal{S}^2$. This observation model may be understood as observing a realization of the Gaussian process $\{\int h(\phi_1,\phi_2)[f_\mathfrak{g}(\phi_1,\phi_2)\mathrm{d}(\phi_1,\phi_2)
+\sigma\,\mathrm{d}W(\phi_1,\phi_2)]\}_{h \in L_2(\mathcal{S}^2)}$ defined analogously to (3.1), or equivalently, as observing each coefficient of $f_\mathfrak{g}$ in an orthonormal basis of $L_2(\mathcal{S}^2)$ with i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ noise.

We choose as our orthonormal basis the real spherical harmonics $$h_{lm}(\phi_1, \phi_2) \quad \text{ for } l=0,1,2,\ldots \text{ and }
m=-l,-l+1,\ldots,l-1,l.$$ We assume that $f:\mathcal{S}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ has a finite bandlimit $L \geq 1$ in this basis, that is, it takes the form $$f(\phi_1,\phi_2)=\sum_{l=0}^L \sum_{m=-l}^l \theta_m^{(l)}h_{lm}(\phi_1,\phi_2).\tag{4.1}$$ We may then represent $f$ by its vector of real spherical harmonic coefficients $$\theta=(\theta_m^{(l)}:\,l=0,\ldots,L \text{ and } m=-l,\ldots,l) \in \mathbb{R}^d,
\qquad d=(L+1)^2.$$ This subspace of bandlimited functions is closed under $\mathsf{SO}(3)$-rotations of $\mathcal{S}^2$, and we review the forms of $h_{lm}$ and of the rotational action on the basis coefficients in Appendix D.2.

Denote the Fourier coefficients of the true function $f$ by $\theta_* \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Define the complex Fourier coefficients $$u^{(0)}(\theta)=\theta^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad
u^{(l)}(\theta)=\theta_1^{(l)}+\mathbf{i}\theta_2^{(l)}=r_l(\theta)e^{\mathbf{i}
\lambda_l(\theta)} \in \mathbb{C},$$ where $(r_l(\theta),\lambda_l(\theta))$ for $l \geq 1$ are the magnitude and phase of $u^{(l)}(\theta)$. Write as shorthand $$r_{l,l',l''}(\theta)=r_l(\theta)r_{l'}(\theta)r_{l''}(\theta),
\qquad \lambda_{l,l',l''}(\theta)=\lambda_l(\theta)-\lambda_{l'}(\theta)
-\lambda_{l''}(\theta).$$ Here $\lambda_{l,l',l''}(\theta)$ are the elements of the Fourier bispectrum of $\theta$.
